To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the attention mechanisms of attention-based encoder decoder networks are task-specific; and 2) the mechanisms are independent of the architecture used for the recurrent or feed-forward encoder and decoder.

(a) attention mechanisms are formed by combining temporal (independent from input) and input driven (independent from position in sequence) components, (b) the relative contributions of these components are task specific, and (c) these findings hold for both recurrent and feed forward architectures.

1) attention matrices are a function of temporal and input-driven components; 2) temporal component of the hidden state depends on the architecture of encoder-decoder; 3) input-driven components of the hidden state are independent of architecture.

the attention mechanism in encoder-decoder networks is a powerful tool for aligning hidden states across the encoder and decoder, but that it can be used in different ways depending on the task.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we show that attention is a powerful tool that is able to adapt to the needs of the particular task.
we provide a novel way of decomposing encoder and decoder states into temporal and input-driven components.
attention is a mechanism that allows the network to focus on the most relevant part of an input sequence.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the temporal component is the main driver of attention matrices.
attention-based networks rely on temporal and input-driven components of the encoder hidden states to form attention matrices.
attention is not a single mechanism, and different tasks require different attention mechanisms to succeed.
